claim: MicroRNA-122 (miR-122) is the most abundant microRNA in hepatocytes.
source: MicroRNA-122 (miR-122) is the most abundant microRNA in hepatocytes and a central player in liver biology and disease.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citation to Lagos-Quintana et al., 2002 in the introduction.

claim: Restoration of miR-122 levels in hepatoma cells markedly enhanced the activation of interferons (IFNs) in response to a variety of viral nucleic acids or simulations.
source: Restoration of miR-122 levels in hepatoma cells markedly enhanced the activation of interferons (IFNs) in response to a variety of viral nucleic acids or simulations, especially in response to hepatitis C virus RNA and poly (I:C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: miR-122 downregulated the phosphorylation (Tyr705) of STAT3.
source: Mechanistically, miR-122 downregulated the phosphorylation (Tyr705) of STAT3, thereby removing the negative regulation of STAT3 on IFN-signaling.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3B showing that miR-122 overexpression inhibited p-STAT3 (Tyr705).

claim: STAT3 represses IFN expression by inhibiting interferon regulatory factor 1 (IRF1).
source: STAT3 represses IFN expression by inhibiting interferon regulatory factor 1 (IRF1), whereas miR-122 targets MERTK, FGFR1 and IGF1R, three receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) that directly promote STAT3 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing that STAT3 knockdown increased IRF1 expression and that STAT3 binds to IRF1 promoter/enhancers (Figure 5).

claim: miR-122 targets MERTK, FGFR1 and IGF1R, three receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) that directly promote STAT3 phosphorylation.
source: STAT3 represses IFN expression by inhibiting interferon regulatory factor 1 (IRF1), whereas miR-122 targets MERTK, FGFR1 and IGF1R, three receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) that directly promote STAT3 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assays (Figure 7A), knockdown experiments (Figure 7C), and Western blot analysis (Figure 7D).

claim: HepG2 has a relatively strong innate immunity compared to that of Huh7 and Huh7.5.1.
source: By measuring the induction of phosphorylated STAT1 (p-STAT1, a marker of IFN signaling activation), melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5, an interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) that is markedly induced upon IFN signaling activation), and IFN mRNAs (IFN-β, type I; IL-29 and IL-28, type III), we found that HepG2 has a relatively strong innate immunity compared to that of Huh7 and Huh7.5.1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 1—source data 1), and may be relatively close to the primary human hepatocytes in innate immune response (Israelow et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B and citations to Israelow et al., 2014 and Thomas et al., 2012.

claim: HCV RNA (JFH1 and SGR-JFH1), double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) mimetic poly(I:C) and 5′ triphosphate hairpin RNA (3p-hpRNA) induced strong IFN responses in HepG2 cells.
source: In addition to HCV RNA (JFH1 and SGR-JFH1), double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) mimetic poly(I:C) and 5′ triphosphate hairpin RNA (3p-hpRNA) also induced strong IFN responses, specifically of type III IFNs (IL-29 and IL-28) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Transfection with RNAs extracted from HBV replicons, in vitro transcribed HBV εRNA, viral DNA motif derived from HSV (HSV-60), or U-rich single-stranded RNA derived from HIV (ssRNA40) only induced weak IFN activation in HepG2 cells.
source: By contrast, transfection with RNAs extracted from HepG2 cells harbouring transient (HBV1.3) or stable (HBV2.15) HBV replicons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 1—source data 2), in vitro transcribed HBV εRNA (Sato et al., 2015) (a structure in pre-genomic HBV RNA that has been shown to induce type III IFNs), viral DNA motif derived from the herpes simplex virus (HSV-60), or U-rich single-stranded RNA derived from HIV (ssRNA40) only induced weak IFN activation (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1A and citation to Sato et al., 2015.

claim: miR-122 overexpression markedly increased the IFN induction in response to almost all of the stimuli tested, but did not impact the IFN expression in cells without stimulation.
source: Surprisingly, miR-122 overexpression markedly increased the IFN induction in response to almost all of the stimuli we tested, but did not impact the IFN expression in cells without stimulation (Figure 1C–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Figure 1—source data 5).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and ELISA data shown in Figures 1C-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The activating effect of miR-122 on IFN induction was more remarkable in cells treated with HCV RNA (both JFH1 and SGR-JFH1) or poly(I:C).
source: Notably, within all groups, the activating effect of miR-122 on IFN induction was more remarkable in cells treated with HCV RNA (both JFH1 and SGR-JFH1) or poly(I:C) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), both of which can form dsRNA structures (Saito et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and citation to Saito et al., 2008.

claim: ISGs downstream of the JAK-STAT cascade, including MDA5, RIG-I, and the chemokines CXCL9 and CXCL10, were greatly increased by miR-122 overexpression.
source: In addition, ISGs downstream of the JAK-STAT cascade, including MDA5, retinoic acid inducible gene I (RIG-I), and the chemokines CXCL9 and CXCL10, were also greatly increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 1—source data 7), suggesting that the entire IFN pathway was upregulated.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The HCV RNA level was only slightly higher (~1.5 fold increase) in miR-122-treated cells than in control-treated cells.
source: However, the HCV RNA level was only slightly higher (~1.5 fold increase) in miR-122-treated cells than in control-treated cells (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1), even though HCV translation was increased by more than 20-fold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2A and luciferase assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HCV translation was increased by more than 20-fold by miR-122 overexpression.
source: However, the HCV RNA level was only slightly higher (~1.5 fold increase) in miR-122-treated cells than in control-treated cells (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1), even though HCV translation was increased by more than 20-fold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Western blot data in Figure 2D.

claim: When the HCV RNA transfection dose rose from 1 μg to 3 μg per ml, the intracellular viral RNA increased 6-fold, but the expression of IFNs only doubled.
source: Analysis of the effect of HCV RNA dosage on IFN activation showed that when the transfection dose rose from 1 μg to 3 μg per ml, the intracellular viral RNA increased 6-fold, but the expression of IFNs only doubled (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The effect of miR-122 on IFN induction was not due to the increase in HCV RNA.
source: Therefore, the effect of miR-122 on IFN induction was not due to the increase in HCV RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that HCV RNA levels increased only slightly while IFN induction increased dramatically.

claim: Binding to HCV RNA is not required for the activating effect of miR-122 on IFNs.
source: By contrast, the mutation did not reduce the activating effect of miR-122 on p-STAT1 (Figure 2D) and IFNs (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 4), indicating that binding to HCV RNA is not required for the activating effect of miR-122 on IFNs.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2D and qRT-PCR data in Figure 2E using mutant HCV RNA (JFH1-M).

claim: miR-122 did not promote the induction of p-STAT1 in HepG2 cells treated with either IFN-β or IL-29.
source: However, we found that miR-122 did not promote the induction of p-STAT1 in HepG2 cells treated with either IFN-β or IL-29 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the effect of miR-122 on IFN signaling was not achieved by the suppression of these JAK inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: miR-122 did not inhibit the mRNA expression of five tested SOCS genes (SOCS1–5).
source: In line with this hypothesis, miR-122 did not inhibit the mRNA expression of five tested SOCS genes (SOCS1–5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: miR-122 significantly repressed the activity of STAT3.
source: When we investigated the effects of miR-122 on several immunity-related signaling pathways using the Multi-Pathway Reporter Arrays, we found that miR-122 significantly repressed the activity of STAT3 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 2), a known negative regulator of type I IFN-mediated antiviral responses (Ho and Ivashkiv, 2006; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 3A and citations to Ho and Ivashkiv, 2006 and Wang et al., 2011.

claim: miR-122 overexpression strongly inhibited tyrosine (Tyr705) phosphorylation of STAT3 (p-STAT3) but did not affect the total STAT3 protein level.
source: Intriguingly, miR-122 overexpression strongly inhibited tyrosine (Tyr705) phosphorylation of STAT3 (p-STAT3) but did not affect the total STAT3 protein level, independent of HCV RNA or poly(I:C) stimulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 3B.

claim: STAT3 knockdown greatly increased IFN production in response to HCV RNA or poly(I:C) stimulation.
source: Excitingly, STAT3 knockdown greatly increased IFN production (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—source datas 4–6) and p-STAT1 induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) in response to HCV RNA or poly(I:C) stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figures 3D and 3F, ELISA data in Figure 3E, and Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Blocking of STAT3 phosphorylation using the chemical inhibitor S3I-201 or the natural compound cryptotanshinone (CTS) increased the IFN response.
source: Furthermore, blocking of STAT3 phosphorylation using the chemical inhibitor S3I-201 (Siddiquee et al., 2007) or the natural compound cryptotanshinone (CTS) (Shin et al., 2009) also increased the IFN response (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, Figure 3—source data 7).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data in Figures 3G and 3H, and citations to Siddiquee et al., 2007 and Shin et al., 2009.

claim: miR-122 regulates IFN activation by repressing STAT3 phosphorylation.
source: Therefore, these data demonstrate that miR-122 regulates IFN activation by repressing STAT3 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing miR-122 reduces p-STAT3 and that reducing p-STAT3 increases IFN activation.

claim: Both miR-122 overexpression and STAT3 knockdown substantially increased IRF1 expression at 24 hr post HCV RNA transfection.
source: Both miR-122 overexpression and STAT3 knockdown substantially increased IRF1 expression at 24 hr post HCV RNA transfection, but did not significantly impact the expression of the other transcription factors (data on IRF7 is not shown because it was barely detected) (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4A.

claim: STAT3 knockdown increased IRF1 activation very early or even in unstimulated cells.
source: Analysis of the protein expression of IRF1 and IRF3 at different time after HCV RNA stimulation showed that STAT3 knockdown increased IRF1 activation very early or even in unstimulated cells (Figure 4B), suggesting that IRF1 upregulation might account for the increased IFN activation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4B.

claim: IRF1 overexpression was able to trigger IFN expression and STAT1 phosphorylation directly in the absence of stimulus.
source: As expected, IRF1 overexpression was able to trigger IFN expression (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 2) and STAT1 phosphorylation (Figure 4D) directly in the absence of stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4C and Western blot data in Figure 4D.

claim: IRF1 overexpression primarily induced IFN-λ expression.
source: Consistent with the report showing that IRF1 is specifically required for IFN-λ activation (Odendall et al., 2014), IRF1 overexpression primarily induced IFN-λ expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4C and citation to Odendall et al., 2014.

claim: IRF1 induced both STAT1 phosphorylation and MDA5 expression in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Notably, IRF1 induced both STAT1 phosphorylation and MDA5 expression in a dose-dependent manner, and even a small amount of IRF1 evidently increased p-STAT1 and MDA5 expression (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4E.

claim: IRF1 is the major inducer of p-STAT1 among seven known transcriptional regulators of IFN-β.
source: Comparing IRF1 activity to that of six known transcriptional regulators of IFN-β (Panne et al., 2007) also revealed that IRF1 is the major inducer of p-STAT1 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4F and citation to Panne et al., 2007.

claim: STAT3 knockdown did not increase the induction of IRF1 by either IFN-β or IL-29.
source: In our system, however, STAT3 knockdown did not increase the induction of IRF1 by either IFN-β or IL-29 (Figure 4G), suggesting that STAT3 might inhibit IRF1 through another mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 4G.

claim: Seven STAT3 binding clusters (BS1 to BS7) have been identified on the IRF1 gene locus.
source: We noticed that seven STAT3 binding clusters (BS1 to BS7) have been identified on the IRF1 gene locus, and that three clusters (BS1, BS3 and BS4) possess conserved STAT3-binding motifs (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data from the UCSC Genome Browser.

claim: STAT3 strongly bound to BS1, BS2, BS3 and BS4 sites in HepG2 cells.
source: Interestingly, STAT3 strongly bound to BS1, BS2, BS3 and BS4 sites, whereas p-STAT3 bound to BS2, BS3 and BS4 but not BS1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 5B.

claim: p-STAT3 bound to BS2, BS3 and BS4 but not BS1 in HepG2 cells.
source: Interestingly, STAT3 strongly bound to BS1, BS2, BS3 and BS4 sites, whereas p-STAT3 bound to BS2, BS3 and BS4 but not BS1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 5B.

claim: Both phosphorylated and un-phosphorylated STAT3 participate in the regulation of IRF1.
source: These data indicate that both phosphorylated and un-phosphorylated STAT3 participate in the regulation of IRF1.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data showing both STAT3 and p-STAT3 bind to IRF1 regulatory regions.

claim: The activities of the P1 and P7 constructs were substantially greater than those of all of the other IRF1 promoter/enhancer constructs.
source: Consistent with previous studies demonstrating that the IRF1 promoter is located immediately upstream of the IRF1 transcriptional start site (TSS1 in Figure 5A) (Harada et al., 1994), the activities of the P1 and P7 constructs were substantially greater than those of all of the other constructs (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 5C and citation to Harada et al., 1994.

claim: The activities of constructs P1, P7 and P4 were obviously increased by poly(I:C) stimulation.
source: Notably, the activities of constructs P1, P7 and P4 were obviously increased by poly(I:C) stimulation, indicating that activating elements are mainly located within P1 (BS1) and P4 (BS4).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of STAT3 in HepG2 cells upregulated the activities of P1, P7 and P4 constructs.
source: As expected, knockdown of STAT3 in HepG2 cells upregulated the activities of all three constructs (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 2), whereas overexpression of STAT3 in 293FT cells (in which the endogenous p-STAT3 level is relatively low) inhibited their activities (Figure 5E, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Overexpression of STAT3 in 293FT cells inhibited the activities of P1, P7 and P4 constructs.
source: As expected, knockdown of STAT3 in HepG2 cells upregulated the activities of all three constructs (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 2), whereas overexpression of STAT3 in 293FT cells (in which the endogenous p-STAT3 level is relatively low) inhibited their activities (Figure 5E, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 5E.

claim: Mutation of the predicted STAT3-binding site within P1 resulted in an obvious decrease in the reporter activity and abolished the response of the P1 promoter to poly(I:C) stimulation.
source: In HepG2 cells, mutation of the predicted STAT3-binding site within P1 resulted in an obvious decrease in the reporter activity and abolished the response of the P1 promoter to poly(I:C) stimulation (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 4), suggesting that this site is also essential for the transcriptional activation of P1 in HepG2 cells.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 5G.

claim: The mutations (P1-M and P4-M) obviously reduced the binding of STAT3 to both P1 and P4 promoters.
source: As expected, the mutations (P1-M and P4-M) obviously reduced the binding of STAT3 to both P1 and P4 promoters (Figure 5I), but STAT3 still binds to the mutant promoters, especially that of P4.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data in Figure 5I.

claim: RELA knockdown significantly reduced the binding of STAT3 to BS1′.
source: Interestingly, RELA knockdown significantly reduced the binding of STAT3 to BS1′, even more effectively than knockdown of STAT3 itself (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, Figure 5—source data 6), suggesting that STAT3 could also bind to P1 in a RELA-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: STAT3 represses IRF1 activation by binding to the promoter and enhancers of the IRF1 gene.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that STAT3 represses IRF1 activation by binding to the promoter and enhancers of the IRF1 gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined ChIP and luciferase reporter data showing STAT3 binds to IRF1 regulatory regions and represses their activity.

claim: Twenty genes were obviously downregulated by miR-122 in HepG2 cells.
source: The qRT-PCR data confirmed that 20 genes were obviously downregulated by miR-122 (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 2), but the remaining five genes were barely detected or were unchanged (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6B.

claim: Knocking down most genes (except for FGFR1, DSTYK, ABL2 and OSMR) reduced the p-STAT3 level.
source: While knocking down most genes (except for FGFR1, DSTYK, ABL2 and OSMR) reduced the p-STAT3 level, the knockdown of ten genes (MERTK, EPO, FGFR1, JAK3, PKM2, IGF2, IL8, ABL2, MAK3K3 and FGF11) appeared to increase the p-STAT1 level (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6C.

claim: The knockdown of ten genes (MERTK, EPO, FGFR1, JAK3, PKM2, IGF2, IL8, ABL2, MAK3K3 and FGF11) appeared to increase the p-STAT1 level.
source: While knocking down most genes (except for FGFR1, DSTYK, ABL2 and OSMR) reduced the p-STAT3 level, the knockdown of ten genes (MERTK, EPO, FGFR1, JAK3, PKM2, IGF2, IL8, ABL2, MAK3K3 and FGF11) appeared to increase the p-STAT1 level (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 6C.

claim: p-STAT1 upregulation was accompanied by an increase in IFN expression.
source: The qRT-PCR data confirmed that p-STAT1 upregulation was accompanied by an increase in IFN expression (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6D.

claim: The overexpression of FGFR1, IGF1R, MERTK, JAK3 and FGF11 clearly upregulated p-STAT3 levels in Huh7 or 293FT cells.
source: In Huh7 or 293FT cells, however, the overexpression of most of the genes increased p-STAT3 levels (Figure 6F,G). In particular, FGFR1, IGF1R, MERTK, JAK3 and FGF11 clearly upregulated p-STAT3 levels (Figure 6F,G), even though the effect was slightly different in the two cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: Nine genes, including IGF1R, PKM2, MAP3K3, IL1RN, MERTK, EPO, FGFR1, DSTYK and FGF11, were directly repressed by miR-122.
source: In addition to the four positive controls, seven sites from six genes (IL1RN, MERTK, EPO, FGFR1, DSTYK and FGF11) could be significantly repressed by miR-122 and mutating of their 'seed' sequence largely or completely abolished the response to miR-122 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 1). Therefore, nine genes, including the three known miR-122 targets, were directly repressed by miR-122.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 7A.

claim: The mRNA expression of six genes (IGF1R, PKM2, FGFR1, FGF11, IGF2 and MERTK) was significantly higher (>2 fold) in the HepG2 cells than in the normal liver.
source: Interestingly, the mRNA expression of six genes (IGF1R, PKM2, FGFR1, FGF11, IGF2 and MERTK) was significantly higher (>2 fold) in the HepG2 cells than in the normal liver (Figure 7B, Figure 7—source data 2), suggesting that these genes might account for the persistent STAT3 activation in HepG2 cells.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7B.

claim: MERTK and IGF1R knockdown markedly decreased the p-STAT3 level.
source: Remarkably, while PKM2 and IGF2 knockdown moderately decreased p-STAT3 levels, MERTK and IGF1R knockdown markedly decreased the p-STAT3 level (Figure 7C), indicating that MERTK and IGF1R might be the key factors that mediate miR-122's regulation of p-STAT3.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 7C.

claim: miR-122 overexpression sharply inhibited the protein expression of three RTKs: MERTK, FGFR1 and IGF1R.
source: Consistent with the decreased mRNA expression, miR-122 overexpression sharply inhibited the protein expression of three RTKs: MERTK, FGFR1 and IGF1R (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 7D.

claim: miR-122 suppresses STAT3 phosphorylation mainly by targeting RTK signaling.
source: Therefore, these results suggest that miR-122 suppresses STAT3 phosphorylation mainly by targeting RTK signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing miR-122 targets multiple RTKs that promote STAT3 phosphorylation.

claim: Knockdown of STAT3 reduced the expression of half of the 20 identified genes to different extents.
source: Surprisingly, knockdown of STAT3 reduced the expression of half of these genes to different extents (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—source data 3), suggesting that STAT3 also regulates them in a positive feedback manner.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: miR-122 is responsible for restricting STAT3 phosphorylation to a low level in normal hepatocytes.
source: According to this model, miR-122 is responsible for restricting STAT3 phosphorylation to a low level in normal hepatocytes, which enables a robust innate immune defense upon infection.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined experimental findings.

claim: Antisense-mediated inhibition of miR-122 in chimpanzees with chronic HCV infection resulted in a rapid decline of the endogenous IFN pathway in the liver.
source: In chimpanzees with chronic HCV infection, antisense-mediated inhibition of miR-122 resulted in a rapid decline of the endogenous IFN pathway in the liver (Lanford et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Lanford et al., 2010.

claim: The expression of interferon-regulated genes was reduced to the normal level even when therapy did not completely eradicate detectable viral RNA in miR-122 inhibition studies.
source: Further evidence to support such role are data showing that the expression of interferon-regulated genes was reduced to the normal level even when therapy did not completely eradicate detectable viral RNA (Lanford et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Lanford et al., 2010.

claim: Decreased miR-122 levels in individuals with hepatitis C are associated with a poor response to IFN therapy.
source: In addition, liver biopsy studies showed that decreased miR-122 levels in individuals with hepatitis C are associated with a poor response to IFN therapy (Sarasin-Filipowicz et al., 2009; Urban et al., 2010), suggesting that abundant miR-122 in hepatocytes promotes cellular responses to IFN treatment.
evidence: This is cited from Sarasin-Filipowicz et al., 2009 and Urban et al., 2010.

claim: miR-122 deletion in mice resulted in an upregulation of FGFR1 and IGF1R, but not of STAT3.
source: Supportive of such mechanism is the evidence that miR-122 deletion in mice resulted in an upregulation of FGFR1 and IGF1R, but not of STAT3 (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Tsai et al., 2012.

claim: HCV can sequester miR-122 through a 'sponge' effect and globally reduces miR-122 targets.
source: Interestingly, HCV can sequester miR-122 through a 'sponge' effect and globally reduces miR-122 targets (Luna et al., 2015), suggesting that HCV-induced miR-122 sequestration may be another mechanism that results in STAT3 activation and immune tolerance.
evidence: This is cited from Luna et al., 2015.

claim: miR-122 might primarily contribute to HCV translation rather than the protection of HCV RNA.
source: These data suggest that miR-122 might primarily contribute to HCV translation (as has also been suggested by other studies (Henke et al., 2008; Jangra et al., 2010; Roberts et al., 2011)), rather than the protection of HCV RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing HCV RNA increased only slightly while translation increased dramatically, and is supported by citations to Henke et al., 2008; Jangra et al., 2010; Roberts et al., 2011.

claim: Knockdown of XRN1 resulted in a 2.7-fold increase in HCV translation (GLuc activity).
source: Although miR-122 overexpression led to a more than 20-fold increase in HCV translation (as determined by GLuc activity), knockdown of XRN1 (a 5′ exonuclease that was reported to mediate HCV decay (Li et al., 2013b)) only resulted in a 2.7-fold increase in GLuc activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and citation to Li et al., 2013b.

claim: miR-122 plays a dual role in the HCV life cycle.
source: In particular, we demonstrate that miR-122 plays a dual role in the HCV life cycle, which should be paid attention to in treating HCV.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings that miR-122 both promotes HCV translation and enhances innate immunity.

claim: STAT3 is a key negative regulator in the miR-122–RTKs/STAT3–IRF1–IFNs circuitry.
source: On the basis of our finding that STAT3 is a key negative regulator in the miR-122–RTKs/STAT3–IRF1–IFNs circuitry, STAT3 targeting may be a promising strategy for treating hepatitis viruses.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental findings showing STAT3's central role in the regulatory pathway.
